content: Preterm birth occurs in approximately 6% to 10% of all pregnancies and represents a significant complication associated with increased perinatal mortality and morbidity. A history of preterm delivery is a strong predictor of future preterm labor, with earlier preterm births being more likely to recur at a similar gestational age. In acute clinical scenarios, betamimetic agents have been shown to reduce the frequency of uterine contractions or delay preterm birth by 24 to 48 hours. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of prophylactic oral betamimetics in preventing preterm labor and birth in women with singleton pregnancies who are at high risk of preterm delivery. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of October 2010) and relevant reference lists. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials involving singleton pregnancies at high risk of preterm labor, comparing prophylactic oral betamimetics with placebo or other interventions specifically aimed at preventing preterm birth. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. Only one trial, involving 64 women with singleton pregnancies, met the inclusion criteria. This trial compared the oral betamimetic agent isoxsuprine with a placebo. The results showed no significant difference in the rate of perinatal mortality between the two groups (risk ratio [RR] 4.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50 to 45.00). Additionally, there was no evidence that oral betamimetics reduced the incidence of spontaneous preterm labor (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.14 to 8.09) or preterm birth before 37 weeks of gestation. The study also found no significant association between the use of oral betamimetics and adverse side effects severe enough to necessitate discontinuation of therapy (RR 2.51, 95% CI 0.59 to 10.76). Furthermore, no differences were observed in infant outcomes, including birthweight less than 2500 grams (RR 1.74, 95% CI 0.44 to 6.87) or neonatal death (RR 4.74, 95% CI 0.50 to 45.00). While the trial was methodologically sound, the sample size was too small to detect any meaningful differences in neonatal outcomes between the treatment groups. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to either support or refute the use of prophylactic oral betamimetics for the prevention of preterm birth in women with singleton pregnancies who are at high risk of preterm labor. Further research with larger sample sizes is needed to determine the efficacy and safety of this intervention.
